nameStory: The Solitary Sandpiper earned its name from its habit of feeding alone rather than in the large flocks typical of most sandpipers. While other shorebirds gather in chattering groups along mudflats, this independent bird prefers to hunt for food by itself in quiet woodland pools and marshy edges. The name comes directly from the Latin 'solitaria,' meaning 'alone,' perfectly capturing this bird's antisocial dining habits.
description: The Solitary Sandpiper is a medium-sized shorebird about the size of a robin, with long legs and a straight, pointed bill perfect for probing muddy shallows. Its back and wings are dark brown with white spots, while its belly is clean white, giving it a crisp, well-dressed appearance. Unlike most sandpipers that prefer ocean beaches, this bird seeks out freshwater spots like woodland ponds, beaver marshes, and muddy creek edges. When startled, it flies off with distinctive white outer tail feathers flashing like semaphore flags.

idTips.label: White outer tail feathers
idTips.description: When the bird takes flight, watch for bright white outer tail feathers that flash conspicuously against the dark back - this is the most reliable field mark that separates it from similar sandpipers

idTips.label: Dark spotted back
idTips.description: The upper parts appear dark brown or blackish with crisp white spots scattered across the back and wings, creating a polka-dotted pattern visible even at a distance

idTips.label: Greenish-yellow legs
idTips.description: The legs are a distinctive greenish-yellow or olive color, quite different from the bright yellow legs of yellowlegs sandpipers - they look almost muddy in tone

idTips.label: Straight dark bill
idTips.description: The bill is straight, dark, and medium-length - not drooped like a dunlin's or upturned like a yellowlegs', but sturdy enough for probing soft mud

idTips.label: White eye-ring
idTips.description: A thin white ring around the dark eye gives the bird an alert, bright-eyed expression that's often visible through binoculars

idTips.label: Teeter-totter behavior
idTips.description: Like a Spotted Sandpiper, it constantly bobs its rear end up and down while walking, as if keeping time to music only it can hear

habitat: Look for Solitary Sandpipers around freshwater habitats like woodland ponds, beaver marshes, muddy creek edges, and flooded fields rather than ocean beaches. They prefer quiet, secluded spots with soft mud or shallow water where they can probe for aquatic insects and small invertebrates. In New England, they're often found in forested wetlands, farm ponds, and the marshy edges of slow-moving streams.

seasonality.spring: Spring migrants pass through New England from late April through May, often appearing suddenly at woodland ponds after overnight flights. Look for birds in transitional plumage showing a mix of winter and breeding colors.
seasonality.summer: A few non-breeding birds may linger into early summer, but most continue north to breed in the boreal forests of Canada and Alaska. Any summer sightings are likely stragglers or early fall migrants.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings the best viewing opportunities from July through September, with adults arriving first in breeding plumage, followed by juveniles with fresh, crisply spotted plumage.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter - these birds migrate all the way to Central and South America, making any winter sighting in New England highly unusual and noteworthy.

funFact: Unlike every other North American sandpiper that builds ground nests, the Solitary Sandpiper is the only one that nests in trees, taking over old robin or jay nests 4-20 feet off the ground in the spruce forests of northern Canada - making it literally a bird that doesn't follow the flock in any aspect of its life!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Lesser Yellowlegs, but remember 'solitary = dark legs, yellowlegs = yellow legs.' The white outer tail feathers in flight are also a dead giveaway - yellowlegs have barred tails without the bright white edges. If you see it with other sandpipers, it's probably not a Solitary since this bird really does prefer to dine alone.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a sandpiper, this bird actually prefers mud to sand and fresh water to salt water, making it one of the least 'sandy' of all sandpipers. The genus name Tringa comes from an ancient Greek word for a thrush-sized wading bird that Aristotle wrote about over 2,000 years ago.
compareHints: Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones. The white outer tail feathers are unique among New England's Tringa sandpipers - yellowlegs have barred black-and-white tails, while Willets show bold white wing patches instead. Its preference for freshwater and solitary feeding also sets it apart from the more gregarious yellowlegs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either.
Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely.
Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build.
Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species.
